issues.legal_issue: A decree in a specific-performance suit that adjudicates the right to performance and directs conveyance upon payment is final, and later orders extending the time for payment do not amend it or restart the time to appeal.
material_facts: The trial court adjudicated the purchaser’s right to specific performance and directed the vendor to execute a conveyance upon receipt of the balance of the consideration.
The decree provided that if the purchaser did not make the required payment, the suit would stand dismissed.
The vendor appealed after the original appeal period, contending that the decree was preliminary and that later orders extending the payment time had amended it.
issues.conclusion: The decree was not preliminary, and the extensions of time did not amend it. The appeal was therefore barred by limitation when filed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a decree that conclusively adjudicates the right to specific performance is not preliminary merely because performance depends on payment or because default would result in dismissal. An appeal against that decree must be brought within the applicable limitation period; subsequent orders extending the time for payment do not make the appeal one against an amended decree. Sm. Soudamini Das v. Nabatak Mia Bhuiya did not assist the respondent; Jagat Dhish Bhargava v. Jawarhar Lal Bhargava was distinguishable because it concerned delay caused by the court or its officers.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and decree_adjudicates_performance_right and (conveyance_conditional_on_payment or default_causes_dismissal) and later_payment_extension

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: A party appealed from a decree made in a suit seeking specific performance.
predicates.decree_adjudicates_performance_right: The court conclusively determined the claimed right to performance of the contract.
predicates.conveyance_conditional_on_payment: The decree directed conveyance in exchange for payment of the balance due.
predicates.default_causes_dismissal: The decree stated that failure to make the required payment would result in dismissal of the suit.
predicates.later_payment_extension: A court later extended the time allowed for payment without changing the adjudication of the right to performance.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an adjudication of specific-performance rights, payment conditions and later payment extensions do not shift the starting point for the appeal period from the original decree.

issues.legal_issue: A court may condone delay when sufficient cause is established, and the Supreme Court will not interfere with a reasoned exercise of that discretion unless it is manifestly unjust or perverse.
material_facts: The vendor filed an appeal well after the decree and applied for condonation of delay.
The vendor believed the decree was preliminary and that an appeal would become necessary only after the purchaser deposited the balance and the court refused to draw a final decree.
The purchaser sought extensions to make the deposit, and the vendor sought a final decree soon after the deposit was made; after that request was refused, the vendor appealed.
The purchaser filed no affidavit opposing the application for condonation, leaving its factual assertions unrebutted.
The High Court considered the circumstances and found sufficient cause for the delay.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s decision to condone the delay was supported by relevant considerations and was not shown to be manifestly unjust or perverse; the Supreme Court would not interfere with it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act requires sufficient cause for not appealing within time, with the explanation covering the period of delay. Sufficient cause is construed liberally to advance substantial justice when negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not attributable to the applicant. The matter is discretionary, and the Supreme Court is reluctant to interfere unless the exercise is manifestly unjust or perverse. Sitaram Ramacharan v. M. N. Nagarashana and State of West Bengal v. Administrator, Howrah Municipality were relied on; Article 136 framed the Supreme Court’s consideration of interference.

rule.if: appeal_against_lower_court_decision and delayed_appeal and condonation_requested and sufficient_cause_found_on_relevant_facts and (delay_explanation_unrebutted or prompt_action_after_obstacle_removed) and no_negligence_or_bad_faith

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_decision: A party sought appellate review of a lower court decision.
predicates.delayed_appeal: The appeal was filed after the applicable time for appealing had expired.
predicates.condonation_requested: The appellant asked the court to excuse the delay.
predicates.sufficient_cause_found_on_relevant_facts: The court assessed the circumstances and found an adequate explanation for not appealing in time.
predicates.delay_explanation_unrebutted: The opposing party did not file evidence disputing the factual explanation for delay.
predicates.prompt_action_after_obstacle_removed: The appellant acted promptly after the circumstance that had led the appellant to defer appealing was resolved.
predicates.no_negligence_or_bad_faith: The delay was not attributable to the appellant’s negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides.

issues.definition: Where a delayed appellant seeks condonation and the court finds a credible explanation without negligence or bad faith, the condonation decision remains undisturbed unless its exercise is manifestly unjust or perverse.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must establish continuing readiness and willingness to perform, and prolonged delay may justify refusal when granting relief would give the purchaser an unfair advantage, even if time was not of the essence and the purchaser was in possession.
material_facts: The contract contemplated completion within a defined period, but the purchaser did not complete the purchase and repeatedly delayed payment and conveyance.
The vendor repeatedly called on the purchaser to complete the transaction and put the purchaser in possession of substantial parts of the property before the balance was paid.
The purchaser remained in possession without paying for its use and occupation while the balance remained unpaid for many years.
The vendor faced mortgage-related financial pressure and, during the purchaser’s delay, had to sell adjacent property to raise money to meet the relevant dues.
The purchaser persisted in disputes over land and expenses that the courts found did not entitle the purchaser to delay completion.
The High Court concluded that the purchaser had avoided performing her part of the contract and that specific performance should be refused.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to specific performance, and the High Court was justified in dismissing the suit because the purchaser’s delay and conduct would give her an unfair advantage over the vendor.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 16(b) and 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act require the plaintiff to establish the relevant contractual entitlement and continuing readiness and willingness to perform. Specific performance depends on the facts and may be refused where the plaintiff’s failure or inordinate delay in performing disentitles the plaintiff to relief or would confer an unfair advantage. Possession does not invariably prevent refusal of relief. Williams v. Greatrex was distinguished on its facts.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaintiff_not_continuously_ready_willing and inordinate_performance_delay and (vendor_repeatedly_sought_completion or purchaser_retained_unpaid_possession) and relief_would_give_unfair_advantage

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff asked a court to compel performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_not_continuously_ready_willing: The plaintiff did not establish continuing readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s contractual obligations.
predicates.inordinate_performance_delay: The plaintiff substantially delayed performing those obligations.
predicates.vendor_repeatedly_sought_completion: The vendor made repeated requests for the purchaser to complete the transaction.
predicates.purchaser_retained_unpaid_possession: The purchaser remained in possession of property before paying the full consideration.
predicates.relief_would_give_unfair_advantage: Granting the requested order would place the plaintiff in an unfairly advantageous position relative to the defendant.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, substantial delay and lack of continuing readiness and willingness may support refusal where the surrounding conduct, including any unpaid possession, would make enforcement unfair.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s financial readiness to perform may be shown by the ability to raise the required funds and does not necessarily require possession of the money or a completed financing arrangement, but the purchaser must prove that ability.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed that she would obtain the balance of the consideration by selling ornaments but did not testify to establish that claim.
The purchaser did not make the required payment when first directed and sought extensions and further orders before eventually depositing the balance.
The record did not establish that the purchaser had sufficient assets or another demonstrated means to obtain the funds when performance was required.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser failed to establish that she could meet the financial obligation, supporting the finding that she was not ready and willing to perform.
issues.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness in a specific-performance claim include the ability to meet the financial obligation, but the plaintiff need not already possess the money or prove a concluded financing scheme if able to raise it when performance is due. Jitendra Nath Roy v. Smt. Maheshwari Bose and Bank of India Ltd. v. Jamsetji A. H. Chinoy were considered.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and financial_performance_required and ability_to_raise_funds_not_proved and repeated_failure_to_pay_when_required

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff asked a court to compel performance of a contract.
predicates.financial_performance_required: Performance required the plaintiff to pay money.
predicates.ability_to_raise_funds_not_proved: The plaintiff did not establish that the required money could be obtained when performance was due.
predicates.repeated_failure_to_pay_when_required: The plaintiff failed to pay when directed and sought further time or orders before paying.

issues.definition: A purchaser who must pay to perform must establish an ability to obtain the funds when due, and repeated nonpayment combined with no proof of that ability means financial readiness is not established.
